content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered mower with an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. When using that machine, you need to manually drive it around the perimeter of your yard to build a virtual map. Once everything is set up, it will automatically perform mowing work according to the schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be the easier-to-use choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how the two machines understand your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK reference station for positioning. Its setup process required me to manually drive the mower along the boundary on my iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Through three cameras, the mower can automatically draw a map of the lawn and navigate without the need to bury boundary wires or set up a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method did take longer to build my initial map. However, I think for people who are less inclined to fiddle with and tweak tech products, this approach may be simpler.

To test this idea, I had my mum, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported that everything worked well. But I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to manually drive a robot all the way around the boundary, and then manually mark out the areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping did cause one small quirk in my front yard. There is no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's lawn, so the TerraMow initially included part of their yard in my map.

I marked the area as a no-go zone in the app to fix the problem. However, for lawns without a visually clear boundary, you may need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping process.

Viewing through the mower's camera

The TerraMow's camera also brings one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the iPhone mirroring feature on my Mac to keep that view open in a large window. This way I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun, and occasionally explains why it slowed down or avoided something. The Anthbot M9 does not offer an equivalent camera view.

The two iPhone apps are actually quite similar in many of their design concepts. Both let you schedule working times, adjust mowing behaviour, set up zones, mark areas to avoid, and remotely control the mower.

TerraMow has a particularly excellent variation on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed control mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually operating the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run on schedule without any intervention. However, TerraMow's joystick is truly impressive when tidying up missed patches.

Sometimes it almost feels like I am controlling the robot with my mind (and in a pleasant way). I can hold the iPhone down at my side, barely moving my thumb as I walk beside the mower, and the machine follows my commands.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground and produced more noise while working.

I wouldn't describe the TerraMow as loud. However, the difference between the two is still noticeable. The Anthbot operates extremely quietly, making it easy to forget it is running, even when it is mowing after dark using its headlight.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built. It is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage in the box that covers the charging base, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I relied on it to run for several weeks in a row without having to take over the routine mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up occasionally works against it.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you cannot perform other operations in the app.

I also ran into an interesting edge case after several days of continuous rain. Puddles formed in parts of the yard, and the TerraMow rightly avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the skipped circular zone, the grass subsequently grew taller. After a while, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches as something to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, the area still wasn't mown.

I solved the problem by using the remote control feature in the app to manually drive the mower through the taller grass. Once that patch returned to normal lawn condition, the automatic mowing function resumed as usual in that area.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow reach the boundaries more reliably. Tall grass growing along indistinct edges might otherwise be treated as obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on the boundaries and obstacles I define myself. This requires more work up front, but it also prevents the map from changing its mind and avoiding a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

Having used both systems, for most people, I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying boundary wires wasn't an option, and installing an RTK reference station adds another piece of hardware that needs to be positioned, powered, and maintained. TerraMow does away with both.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping took longer, an invisible property line had to be manually corrected, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 delivers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a fun live camera view, and the best manual control experience I have used in a robotic mower app.

I do enjoy gardening, but mowing is the repetitive part of it. Handing that task over to a robot frees up more time for landscaping, edging, and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs well enough at this job to earn my recommendation, especially for users who want robotic mowing without burying wires, installing an RTK antenna, or manually mapping out the whole yard with an iPhone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently priced at $999 on Amazon, and you can get it by applying a $200 coupon on the site. You can also find the product on TerraMow's official website.
